concepts.definition: A single wrong reading that is very different from the readings next to it.
concepts.example: In the sequence 100, 100, 350, 100, the 350 is an outlier.
concepts.pitfall: Accepting every reading as correct and making a decision from it straight away.

concepts.definition: The sum of all the values divided by how many there are; it takes the outlier into itself.
concepts.pitfall: Thinking the average has cleaned up the outlier: a wrong reading spoils the result.

concepts.definition: The middle value once the values are sorted; outliers at the ends are not chosen.
concepts.example: In the sorted list 100, 100, 100, 100, 350, the middle one is 100.
concepts.pitfall: Forgetting that the median is fooled too if the wrong values are more than half the window.

concepts.definition: An array that holds the last N readings; a new reading is written in place of the oldest one.
concepts.example: pencere[sira] = x; sira = (sira + 1) % N; goes back to the start when it reaches the end of the array.
concepts.pitfall: Forgetting % N, or not filling the window with the first reading.

concepts.definition: The median filter does not react to a real change straight away; the old value stays until the new value is the majority of the window.
concepts.example: If N = 5 and a measurement is taken every 55 ms, the reaction comes after about 3 × 55 = 165 ms.
concepts.pitfall: Making the window needlessly large: the noise goes down but the system gets slow.

quiz.prompt: Five readings: 80, 82, 81, 400, 80 cm. What is the average of these readings in centimetres?
quiz.explanation: The sum is 80 + 82 + 81 + 400 + 80 = 723; 723 / 5 = 144.6. A single outlier (400) pulled the average up by about 64 cm.

quiz.prompt: What is the median of the same five readings (80, 82, 81, 400, 80) in centimetres?
quiz.explanation: Sorted, they become 80, 80, 81, 82, 400; the middle (3rd) value is 81. The outlier 400 goes to the end of the sorted list and does not affect the median. Compare this with the average (144.6).

quiz.prompt: A 7-element median filter still gives the right result with at most how many outliers in the window?
quiz.explanation: In a window of N elements, the median forgives at most (N − 1) / 2 outliers: (7 − 1) / 2 = 3. If there are four wrong values, the wrong values are the majority and the middle value comes out wrong too.

At the end of the loop, p = {200, 200, 50}. The median of the three values is 200, because in a 3-element window two wrong values are the majority and the median is fooled too (a 3-element window forgives at most 1 wrong value). The average would be 150; the code works out the median.

sira never goes back to the start; after N rounds, pencere[5], pencere[6]... are written outside the array. It should be sira = (sira + 1) % N;. The line pencere[sira] = x; is correct on its own; the overflow comes from the value of sira there.
